# Univariate Hawkes process {#sec-hawkes}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(stelfi)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The model and your data

A univariate Hawkes process (@hawkes) is a model for event *times* where the occurrence of an event temporarily increases the chance of further events. It is described by its conditional intensity, the expected rate of events at time $t$ given everything that has happened before $t$,

$$\lambda(t) = \mu + \alpha \sum_{i:\tau_i<t}\text{exp}(-\beta (t-\tau_i)),$${#eq-hawkes}

where $\tau_1, \tau_2, ...$ are the event times. There are three parameters:

- $\mu$, the **background rate**: the rate at which "spontaneous" events occur, i.e., events not triggered by any earlier event;
- $\alpha$, the **jump** in the intensity immediately after each event; and
- $\beta$, the **decay rate**: how quickly the extra intensity caused by an event dies away. $1/\beta$ is roughly how long (in the units of your times) an event continues to have an influence.

Two derived quantities are usually of most interest:

- the **branching ratio** $\alpha/\beta$, the expected number of events directly triggered by any one event. This must be less than 1 (otherwise the process explodes), and `stelfi` enforces $\alpha \leq \beta$; and
- the expected number of **background events** over the observation period $[0, T]$, which is $\mu T$. The proportion of events that are background events is roughly $1 - \alpha/\beta$.

Plotted below is the conditional intensity of a Hawkes process with $\mu = 0.5$, $\alpha = 1$, and $\beta = 1.5$. The events are shown by the vertical dashes along the x-axis. The intensity jumps by $\alpha$ each time an event occurs and decays exponentially back towards $\mu$ if no event occurs.

```{r, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 8}
#| echo: false
mu <- 0.5; alpha <- 1; beta <- 1.5
tim <- sim_hawkes(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, n = 15)
p <- seq(min(tim), max(tim), length.out = 1000)
lamda <- stelfi:::hawkes_intensity(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, times = tim, p = p)
ggplot(data.frame(x = p, y = lamda), aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    xlab("") + ylab(expression(lambda(t))) +
    geom_line() + theme_minimal() +
    geom_point(data = data.frame(x = tim, y = 0.2), pch = "|", size = 5) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = c("t = 0","t = T"),
                       breaks = seq(min(p), max(p), length.out = 2))
```

### What your data need to look like {#sec-hawkes-data}

`fit_hawkes()` requires a single **numeric vector of event times**. Some things to be aware of:

- **Times must be numeric, sorted, and start near zero.** Dates or date-times (e.g., `POSIXct`) need to be converted to a number, for example with `as.numeric(difftime(x, min(x), units = "days"))`. The **units you choose** (seconds, minutes, days, ...) **set the units of the parameters**: $\mu$ is then events per day (say) and $1/\beta$ is in days. Choose units that make the numbers neither tiny nor huge.
- **No two events can have exactly the same time.** `stelfi` will stop with an error if they do. Ties are very common when times are recorded to the nearest day or minute. You can either drop duplicates (e.g., `unique(times)`), which throws away information, or add a small random amount to each time ("jittering") that is less than the recording resolution, e.g., a random number of seconds within the recorded minute (see @sec-marked-hawkes-applied). If a large proportion of your events are tied the recording resolution is too coarse relative to the speed of the self-excitement and a Hawkes model may not be appropriate.
- **The observation period is assumed to be from $t = 0$ to the last event.** If you watched for events for longer than this, the background rate will be slightly overestimated. Starting the times at the first event (rather than the true start of observation) has a similar small effect.
- **The background rate is assumed to be constant.** If events are more common at certain times of day or year for reasons unrelated to self-excitement, this will be mistaken for self-excitement. See @sec-hawkes-cbf for a model with a time-varying background.
- **Self-excitement is assumed to decay exponentially.** For some processes (e.g., earthquake aftershocks) the influence of an event decays much more slowly than this, which the goodness-of-fit checks in @sec-gof-hawkes will usually reveal.
- **All events are assumed to be of the same type and of the same importance.** See @sec-marked-hawkes if events differ in how much they trigger, and @sec-mhawkes if there are different types of event.

As a rough guide you need at least a hundred or so events to estimate the three parameters with any precision.

## A simulated example {#sec-hawkes-sim}

```{r}
#| echo: false
times <- sim_hawkes(mu = 1.3, alpha = 0.4, beta = 1.5, n = 500)
```

Data were simulated from a Hawkes process with $\mu = 1.3$, $\alpha = 0.4$, and $\beta = 1.5$ over $t \in [0, 500]$ (so the true branching ratio is $\alpha/\beta =$ `r round(0.4/1.5, 3)`). The data are simply a sorted numeric vector of `r length(times)` event times:

```{r}
head(times)
```

### Fitting the model using `stelfi`

To fit a univariate Hawkes model in `stelfi` use `fit_hawkes()` with

- `times`, the vector of event times, and
- `parameters`, a named vector of starting values for $\mu$ (`mu`), $\alpha$ (`alpha`), and $\beta$ (`beta`).

The estimates (and standard errors) are returned by `get_coefs()`.

```{r}
sv <- c(mu = 1, alpha = 0.5, beta = 2)
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = times, parameters = sv)
stelfi <- get_coefs(fit)
stelfi
```

### Comparison with `emhawkes` and `hawkesbow`

The same model can be fitted using the `emhawkes` (@emhawkes) and `hawkesbow` (@hawkesbow) packages. Note that `emhawkes` requires the times *between* events rather than the event times (and here `final_hessian = "stable"` is used, as the default numerical Hessian can fail to give standard errors).

```{r}
#| message: false
## emhawkes
library(emhawkes)
h <- new("hspec", mu = sv[1], alpha = sv[2], beta = sv[3])
inter <- c(0, diff(times))
fit_em <- hfit(object = h, inter_arrival = inter, final_hessian = "stable")
em <- summary(fit_em)$estimate
em
## hawkesbow
library(hawkesbow)
fit_bow <- mle(events = times, kern = "Exponential", end = max(times))
## standard errors from the Hessian
bow <- cbind(Estimate = fit_bow$par,
             "Std. error" = -fit_bow$model$ddloglik(times, max(times)) |>
                 solve() |> diag() |> sqrt())
bow
```

The table below gives the estimates (standard errors in brackets) from each package alongside the true values. Note that `hawkesbow` estimates the branching ratio $\alpha/\beta$ directly, rather than $\alpha$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
fmt <- function(x) paste0(round(x[1], 3), " (", round(x[2], 3), ")")
params <- data.frame(Truth = c(1.3, 0.4, 1.5, round(0.4/1.5, 3)),
                     stelfi = c(apply(stelfi, 1, fmt), "-"),
                     emhawkes = c(apply(em, 1, fmt), "-"),
                     hawkesbow = c(fmt(bow[1, ]), "-", fmt(bow[3, ]), fmt(bow[2, ])))
knitr::kable(t(params), col.names = c("$\\mu$", "$\\alpha$", "$\\beta$", "$\\alpha/\\beta$"),
             escape = FALSE)
```

All three packages give essentially the same answer, and each recovers the true values to within a couple of standard errors. Small differences arise because each package treats the end of the observation period slightly differently.

## An applied example: retweets of a viral tweet {#sec-hawkes-applied}

A [NIWA](https://niwa.co.nz/) scientist [found a working USB stick in the scat of a leopard seal](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12201147) and [tweeted about it](https://twitter.com/niwa_nz/status/1092610541401587712) in the hope of finding its owner. The times of the retweets are available in `stelfi` as `retweets_niwa` (see @sec-data). Retweets are a natural candidate for a Hawkes process: each retweet exposes the tweet to more people, who may then retweet it themselves.

```{r}
data(retweets_niwa, package = "stelfi")
head(retweets_niwa)
```

The data are date-times (`POSIXct`). They are converted to minutes since the first retweet. Retweets are recorded to the nearest second, and a number of retweets share the same second; here duplicate times are simply dropped using `unique()` (see @sec-hawkes-data for an alternative).

```{r}
times <- unique(sort(as.numeric(difftime(retweets_niwa, min(retweets_niwa), units = "mins"))))
length(retweets_niwa) - length(times) ## number of dropped duplicates
```

The histogram below shows the number of retweets per hour from the original tweet to the time (just over two days later) that the owner of the USB stick came forward.

```{r, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 8}
#| echo: false
start <- lubridate::ymd_hms("2019-02-05 02:27:07")
end <- lubridate::ymd_hms("2019-02-07 06:50:08")
hist(retweets_niwa, breaks = "hours", axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "", col = "grey", border = "grey", freq = TRUE)
axis(2, at = c(0, 250))
mtext(2, line = 0, text = "Number of retweets per hour", cex = 0.8)
mtext(1, line = 1, at = c(start, end), text = c("NIWA \n tweeted", "USB owner \n found"), cex = 0.9)
```

To fit the model choose some starting values and supply these, along with the numeric times, to `fit_hawkes()`.

```{r}
sv <- c(mu = 9, alpha = 3, beta = 10)
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = times, parameters = sv)
pars <- get_coefs(fit)
pars
```

From the estimates above (time is in minutes):

 - the expected number of background retweets is $\hat{\mu}T =$ `r round(pars[1,1],3)` $\times$ `r round(max(times),1)` $=$ `r round(pars[1,1] * max(times),1)`, so only around `r round(pars[1,1] * max(times),0)` of the `r length(times)` retweets were "spontaneous" and the remainder were triggered by earlier retweets;
 - the branching ratio is $\hat{\alpha}/\hat{\beta}$ = `r round(pars[2,1]/pars[3,1],2)`, i.e., each retweet directly triggers `r round(pars[2,1]/pars[3,1],2)` further retweets on average; and
 - $1/\hat{\beta}$ = `r round(1/pars[3,1],2)` minutes, so the influence of a retweet largely dies away after around `r round(1/pars[3,1], 0)` minutes.

The `show_hawkes()` function plots the estimated conditional intensity (top) and the data (bottom).

```{r, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 9}
#| message: false
show_hawkes(fit, type = "both")
```

## Goodness-of-fit {#sec-gof-hawkes}

### The idea

The **compensator** $\Lambda(t) = \int_0^{t} \lambda(s) ds$ is the expected number of events up to time $t$ under the fitted model. The random time change theorem (@daley) says that if the model is correct, then the transformed times $\Lambda(\tau_1), \Lambda(\tau_2), ...$ behave like a homogeneous Poisson process with rate 1. Equivalently, the **compensator differences** $\Lambda(\tau_i) - \Lambda(\tau_{i-1})$ should be independent draws from an $\text{Exp}(1)$ distribution. This gives two standard checks:

- a **Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test** of whether the compensator differences follow an $\text{Exp}(1)$ distribution; and
- a **Ljung-Box test** of whether consecutive compensator differences are correlated (they should not be).

Small p-values indicate that the model does not describe the data well. With large datasets these tests will detect even small departures from the model, so the accompanying plots are often more useful than the p-values.

### What a good fit looks like

The compensator differences can be extracted using `compensator_differences()` and tested directly. For the model fitted to the simulated data in @sec-hawkes-sim (where the model is correct):

```{r}
#| echo: false
times_sim <- sim_hawkes(mu = 1.3, alpha = 0.4, beta = 1.5, n = 500)
fit_sim <- fit_hawkes(times = times_sim, parameters = c(mu = 1, alpha = 0.5, beta = 2))
```

```{r}
compensator <- compensator_differences(fit_sim)
stats::ks.test(compensator, "pexp")
stats::Box.test(compensator, type = "Ljung")
```

There is no evidence against the compensator differences being independent $\text{Exp}(1)$ draws. The function `show_hawkes_GOF()` carries out both tests and draws four diagnostic plots:

 - **top left**, the compensator (expected number of events) and the observed cumulative number of events against time, these should lie close to one another;
 - **top right**, a QQ plot of the compensator differences against the $\text{Exp}(1)$ distribution, the points should lie on the line;
 - **bottom left**, a histogram of the compensator differences, which should look like an $\text{Exp}(1)$ distribution; and
 - **bottom right**, consecutive compensator differences (on the probability scale) plotted against each other, which should show no pattern.

```{r, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 9}
show_hawkes_GOF(fit_sim)
```

### The retweet model

```{r, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 9}
show_hawkes_GOF(fit)
```

The compensator follows the observed number of retweets closely (top left), so the model captures the overall rise and fall in retweeting, and the Ljung-Box test gives little evidence of correlation between consecutive compensator differences. The KS test, however, gives a small p-value. With nearly 5000 events the test is very sensitive, and the QQ plot shows the model is broadly adequate: the main departure is that there are *fewer very short gaps* between retweets than the model expects. This is at least partly an artefact of the data, since times are recorded to the nearest second and tied retweets were dropped (@sec-hawkes-data), so very short gaps cannot appear in the data. Note too that the estimated branching ratio is close to 1, which is typical of "viral" behaviour but means the background and self-excitement are hard to separate. Possible next steps are jittering the tied times rather than dropping them, a time-varying background (@sec-hawkes-cbf), or including information on the retweeter, such as their number of followers, as a mark (@sec-marked-hawkes).

## Extension: a time-varying background rate {#sec-hawkes-cbf}

In some applications the background rate itself changes over time, for example with the time of day or the season. Ignoring this can make it look as though there is self-excitement when really events are just more common at certain times. A Hawkes process with a time-varying background replaces $\mu$ in @eq-hawkes with a function $\mu(t)$. This model is fitted in `stelfi` using `fit_hawkes_cbf()` (custom background function).

```{r}
#| echo: false
mut <- function(t) 1 + 0.5 * sin((2 * pi * t) / 365.25)
set.seed(1)
times <- hawkesbow::hawkes(1000, fun = mut, M = 1.5, repr = 0.5, family = "exp", rate = 2)$p
```

Data were simulated (using `hawkesbow`, @hawkesbow) over 1000 days from a Hawkes process with a yearly cycle in the background, $\mu(t) = A + B\,\text{sin}(\frac{2 \pi t}{365.25})$, with $A = 1$ and $B = 0.5$, and self-excitement parameters $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = 2$. As before the data are a sorted vector of `r length(times)` event times.

To fit this model you need to supply both $\mu(t)$ (`background`) and its integral $\int_0^t \mu(s) ds$ (`background_integral`) as functions of a vector of parameters and time. To ensure $\mu(t) > 0$ the parameters are transformed: $A = e^{x}$ and $B = \text{logit}^{-1}(y) A$, so that $0 < B < A$.

```{r}
background <- function(params, t) {
    A <- exp(params[[1]])
    B <- stats::plogis(params[[2]]) * A
    A + B * sin((2 * pi * t) / 365.25)
}
background_integral <- function(params, x) {
    A <- exp(params[[1]])
    B <- stats::plogis(params[[2]]) * A
    (A * x) - B * cos((2 * pi * x) / 365.25)
}
```

These are passed to `fit_hawkes_cbf()` along with the times, starting values for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (`parameters`), and starting values for the background parameters (`background_parameters`).

```{r}
fit <- fit_hawkes_cbf(times = times, parameters = list(alpha = 0.5, beta = 1.5),
                      background = background, background_integral = background_integral,
                      background_parameters = list(1, 1))
get_coefs(fit)
```

`get_coefs()` returns $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as usual, the (transformed) background parameters are in `fit$background_parameters`. These are transformed back to $A$ and $B$ below and compared with the truth.

```{r}
#| echo: false
ab <- get_coefs(fit)[1:2, 1]
A <- exp(fit$background_parameters[1])
B <- plogis(fit$background_parameters[2]) * A
params <- t(data.frame(Truth = c(1, 0.5, 1, 2), stelfi = c(A, B, ab[1], ab[2])))
knitr::kable(params, col.names = c("$A$", "$B$", "$\\alpha$", "$\\beta$"), escape = FALSE, digits = 3)
```

The fitted intensity and goodness-of-fit diagnostics (@sec-gof-hawkes) are shown using `show_hawkes()` and `show_hawkes_GOF()` as before.

```{r, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9}
#| message: false
show_hawkes(fit)
```

```{r, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 9}
show_hawkes_GOF(fit)
```

The KS test and QQ plot show no evidence of lack of fit. The Ljung-Box test, however, gives a small p-value, indicating some correlation between consecutive compensator differences even though the data were simulated from this model. Notice that the background parameters (in particular $B$) are estimated less accurately than the self-excitement parameters: separating a slowly varying background from self-excitement is difficult, and errors in the background show up as correlation in the compensator differences. With real data a result like this suggests revisiting the form of $\mu(t)$.

::: {.callout-note}

When writing your own background function, bear in mind that every extra parameter makes the model harder to fit and that self-excitement and a changing background can be hard to tell apart. Only include a time-varying background if you have a good reason (e.g., a known daily or seasonal cycle), and check that the estimated self-excitement changes when you do.

:::
